phonemes.desc: Pi plus short omicron — the name begins with forward movement.
Mu plus long eta, the sustained middle of the name.
Aspirated theta plus diphthong ευ plus sigma — the sound of forethought and divine knowledge.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pro-meh-THEFS' — the middle syllable is long, and the final diphthong, which carries the accent, glides like the foresight the name denotes.

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *men- 'to think' — root of Greek μῆνις, Latin mens, English 'mind'

kin.label: Titan
kin.form: Son of Iapetus and Clymene; brother of Epimetheus, Atlas, and Menoetius (Hesiod, Theogony 507-518)

pronunciation.note: Promētheus is Tier 1 because the Greek Προμηθεύς contains both stress (acute on the final diphthong) and length (η and the ευ diphthong). His name means 'Forethought,' the opposite of his brother Epimetheus ('Afterthought').

domains.title: The Forethinker
domains.subtitle: Fire, Craft, Foresight, and Human Civilization
domains.lead: Promētheus is the Titan who sided with mortals. He gave humanity fire, taught the arts of civilization, and accepted eternal punishment for his mercy. He is the patron of every outcast intelligence that chooses compassion over obedience.

cards.name: Fire-Bringer
cards.desc: He stole fire from Olympus in a hollow fennel stalk and gave it to humanity — the origin of every technology (Hesiod, Theogony 562-571).

cards.name: Craft and Deception
cards.desc: He tricked Zeus at Mekone, dividing the sacrificial ox so the gods got bones wrapped in fat and mortals kept the meat (Hesiod, Theogony 535-557).

cards.name: Teacher of Humanity
cards.desc: Writing, numbers, astronomy, medicine, shipbuilding, and mining — the arts that make cities possible (Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 450-506).

cards.name: Suffering Savior
cards.desc: Bound to a Caucasian rock, his liver eaten daily by an eagle — the price of his gift to mortals, until Herakles came (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.11).

symbols.name: Fennel stalk
symbols.meaning: The hollow vessel in which fire was smuggled from heaven to earth

symbols.name: Liver
symbols.meaning: The organ that regenerates nightly, making his punishment unending and its relief impossible without a god's consent

symbols.name: Eagle
symbols.meaning: Zeus's own bird, made the instrument of the daily torment

symbols.name: Chains and rock
symbols.meaning: The bondage of the rebel against cosmic order, fastened by Hephaestus against his will

symbols.name: Fire
symbols.meaning: Knowledge, technology, and divine power transferred to mortals — the gift that made humans nearly gods

symbols.name: Ring with stone
symbols.meaning: The ring Zeus made him wear, an iron fetter with a Caucasian stone, so the punishment would never be forgotten

mythology.lead: Prometheus' myths, preserved chiefly by Hesiod and Aeschylus, are Greece's founding meditation on progress and its price: every human power begins as a theft, and every theft must be paid for — in sacrifice, in suffering, and in the knowledge that foresight alone can carry.

myths.title: The Division at Mekone
myths.text: At Mekone, Hesiod tells us in the Theogony (535-557), Prometheus cut up a great ox and arranged two portions: one of fat-wrapped bones that gleamed white and inviting, one of meat and entrails hidden in the ox's paunch. He invited Zeus to choose. Zeus saw through the trick — Hesiod says he knew, and chose the bones anyway, 'and in his heart his soul was angered' — binding mortals thereafter to burn the white bones for the gods on smoking altars. The Works and Days (47-58) makes the same deception explain why the earth feeds us only at the cost of labor. The myth makes sacrifice itself a memorial of a trick: every burnt offering reenacts the moment gods and mortals divided the world between them — and learned to distrust each other.

myths.title: Fire in the Fennel Stalk
myths.text: When Zeus, angry at the division, withheld fire from mortals, Prometheus stole it back — in Hesiod's Theogony (562-571) from the gods themselves, in later art from the forge of Hephaestus or the wheel of the sun-chariot — and carried it to earth hidden in the hollow stalk of a giant fennel. Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound (109-111, 450-506) has the hero list what followed: brick houses instead of caves, shipbuilding, numbers, writing, medicine, divination, mining — the whole armory of civilization purchased with one theft. Fire, the Greeks observed, is the one technology that multiplies all others; giving it to mortals made them nearly godlike, and therefore unbearable. The myth reads progress itself as an act of divine larceny: every human power begins by taking what heaven meant to keep. And Hesiod, tellingly, refuses to celebrate the theft — for him the fire is what made Pandora necessary, technology the first link in a chain that ends in toil.

myths.title: Pandora, the Beautiful Evil
myths.text: Zeus answered the theft with a gift of his own. Hephaestus mixed earth with water and shaped a maiden, Athena dressed her and taught her crafts, Aphrodite poured grace and cruel longing into her breast, Hermes gave her 'a bitch's mind and a thievish character' (Hesiod, Works and Days 60-82), and every god added something — so they named her Pandora, 'All-gifted,' 'because all the Olympians gave her a gift, a bane to industrious men.' The Theogony (570-616) adds the jar she carries, from which fly out the sorrows, toils, and diseases that had never before touched mortal life. The myth is a bitter inversion of Prometheus' gift: where the Titan gave mortals divine power, Zeus sends a divine shape concealing ruin — and, in Hesiod's telling, the first woman becomes the price of fire itself.

myths.title: The Rock and the Eagle
myths.text: For his crimes Zeus bound Prometheus to a pillar or a cliff in the Caucasus and set an eagle — his own bird — to feed each day on the Titan's liver, which grew back each night, making the agony unending (Hesiod, Theogony 521-525 and fr. 343 M-W; Apollodorus, Library 1.7.1; 2.5.11). Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound opens on the very fastening of the chains — Hephaestus, who nails him to the rock, weeps as he works: 'against my will, against my will; necessity compels me' (lines 18, 42). Near the play's close Heracles appears, guided by the sufferer's own prophecy, to shoot the eagle and free him — reconciliation purchased only because the Titan finally knows when to yield. The punishment is framed as the rebel's necessary tuition: power without limit, the gods insist, must end even for Titans.

myths.title: Thetis, and the Fall Zeus Must Avoid
myths.text: Prometheus held one card Zeus could not take: he knew that the sea-goddess Thetis was fated to bear a son greater than his father, and that Zeus or Poseidon, both then suitors, would fall to him (Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 186-192, 756-770; Apollodorus, Library 3.13.5-6). Zeus released him from torment in exchange for the warning; Thetis was married to the mortal Peleus, and her son Achilles became, as Homer sings, the greatest of the Achaeans — yet mortal, and so no threat to the throne. The episode turns knowledge into the coin in which even Zeus must pay: Prometheus suffers, but he is never powerless, because information in his keeping is worth more than thunderbolts. The myth's final lesson is that foresight, even when chained, still bargains with power on equal terms.

lore.syncretism: The Romans adopted him simply as Prometheus, the name borrowed whole; no Latin cult ever attached to him. Early Christian readers split over the figure: to some he was a pagan prefiguration of the suffering savior, to others a warning example of hubris punished. The Renaissance recovered the full text of Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound, and the Titan became the patron of human creativity and revolt — Goethe's 'Prometheus' hymn, Shelley's Prometheus Unbound, Marx's 'Promethean' fire of labor. The modern adjective 'promethean' marks any bold, possibly catastrophic, creative energy; Ridley Scott named an android after him. Few Greek names have been claimed by so many opposing programs — which is perhaps the surest sign that the myth still works.
lore.culturalLegacy: Prometheus is the patron saint of technology and its discontents. Aeschylus' tragedy remains one of the most-read Greek plays; Mary Shelley subtitled Frankenstein 'The Modern Prometheus,' and the name still anchors debates about AI, genetic engineering, and climate: our powers now genuinely seem divine, and the eagle seems to be circling. The ancient Athenians honored him with torch-races from his altar in the Academy — an image of living fire passed hand to hand. Restoring Promētheus, with its long middle syllable and its freighted theta, restores the sound of the name that stands for forethought itself: the gift and the warning in one breath.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Prometheus is the original technologist: he saw what humanity could become and gave it the means. But technology is theft. It takes fire from the gods, time from the future, resources from the earth. The Greek insight is that this theft is not simply good or bad; it is necessary and dangerous.

We live in Prometheus's world. Our powers would seem divine to the Greeks, and our punishments — climate change, nuclear risk, ecological collapse — would seem the eagle returning. The restoration of his name is not nostalgia. It is a warning that every gift has its price, and that forethought must keep pace with power.

lore.archaeology: Prometheus had no great temple, but Athens kept his altar in the Academy, from which torch-races ran to the city (Pausanias 1.30.2). Attic red-figure vases of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE repeatedly show the bound Titan with the eagle at his chest; the theme also rides on Panathenaic prize amphorae. Aeschylus' Prometheus Bound (ca. 460-450 BCE) is itself an archaeological fact of the stage, its hero nailed to a skene-rock before the Athenian audience. The myth's material footprint is thus performative and ceramic rather than architectural — fire, fittingly, leaves no temple.
